title: Das blaue Licht
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 116. Text from Wikisource („Das blaue Licht (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 116 (Das blaue Licht) opens on a soldier discharged penniless after long service and taken in by a witch only on condition of hard labour: three days of digging, wood-splitting, and finally fetching a blue light up from an old dried well. When she tries to seize the light from him before hauling him the rest of the way out, he refuses to let go of it, and she drops him back down and leaves him to die there. Lighting his pipe at the blue light summons a small black servant-spirit bound to whoever does exactly that, and the soldier uses it first to climb out and see the witch hanged, then to have the sleeping princess fetched to his rooms night after night to scrub and scour, as revenge on the king who cast him off without pay. Caught out when a shoe from one of those nights turns up in his room, he is condemned to hang — and asks, as a last favour, to smoke one more pipe, which brings the mannikin to strike down the judges and the king himself, leaving the soldier the kingdom and the princess both. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as daß, gieng, fieng, ward, Rath and Thor.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Soldat, der hatte dem König lange Jahre treu gedient:
sentences.l: There was once a soldier, he had served the king faithfully for long years:
sentences.i: Once there was a soldier who had served the king faithfully for long years.
sentences.n: Es war einmal is the fixed opening of a German tale — literally “it was once,” our “once upon a time.” der hatte is a demonstrative picking up ein Soldat, not a relative pronoun, so the German runs on where English would subordinate. dem König is dative, the person served. The colon does the work of a full stop; this printing uses it that way throughout.

sentences.t: als aber der Krieg zu Ende war und der Soldat, der vielen Wunden wegen, die er empfangen hatte, nicht weiter dienen konnte, sprach der König zu ihm „du kannst heim gehen, ich brauche dich nicht mehr:
sentences.l: but when the war was at an end and the soldier, on account of the many wounds that he had received, could serve no further, the king said to him “you can go home, I do not need you any more:
sentences.i: but when the war came to an end, and the soldier, because of the many wounds he had taken, could serve no longer, the king said to him, “You may go home, I have no more need of you.
sentences.n: der vielen Wunden wegen is a genitive with wegen standing after its noun — “on account of the many wounds”; modern German more often puts wegen first. sprach is the old narrative past of sprechen, “said,” where modern German would use sagte. The king’s speech runs on into the next unit, so the closing quotation mark does not come yet.

sentences.t: Geld bekommst du weiter nicht, denn Lohn erhält nur der, welcher mir Dienste dafür leistet.“
sentences.l: Money you get no more, for pay receives only he who renders me services for it.”
sentences.i: You will get no more money, for only the man who does me service for it receives pay.”
sentences.n: Both clauses put something other than the subject first — Geld, then Lohn — which throws the finite verb into second place and the subject after it. der, welcher is “he who”; welcher is the older relative pronoun where modern German prefers der.

sentences.t: Da wußte der Soldat nicht womit er sein Leben fristen sollte;
sentences.l: Then the soldier did not know with what he was to eke out his life;
sentences.i: Now the soldier did not know how he was to keep himself alive;
sentences.n: sein Leben fristen is a set phrase, to scrape a bare living. sollte here is “was to,” what circumstances required, not moral duty. wußte is the 1857 spelling of wusste.

sentences.t: gieng voll Sorgen fort und gieng den ganzen Tag, bis er Abends in einen Wald kam.
sentences.l: went off full of cares and went the whole day, until he came in the evening into a forest.
sentences.i: he went off full of care and walked the whole day, until at evening he came into a forest.
sentences.n: The subject er is not repeated — German lets the second clause run on from the first subject, and the literal keeps the gap where the idiomatic supplies “he.” gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. Abends is an adverbial genitive of time, “of an evening.”

sentences.t: Als die Finsternis einbrach, sah er ein Licht, dem näherte er sich und kam zu einem Haus, darin wohnte eine Hexe.
sentences.l: When the darkness broke in, he saw a light, to that he drew himself near and came to a house, therein dwelt a witch.
sentences.i: When darkness fell he saw a light; he made toward it and came to a house, and in it dwelt a witch.
sentences.n: einbrechen, of night, is “to fall.” dem is a demonstrative, “to that one,” pointing back to the light and standing first in its clause; sich nähern is reflexive and takes the dative. darin, “therein,” likewise stands first and leaves the verb before its subject.

sentences.t: „Gib mir doch ein Nachtlager und ein wenig Essen und Trinken,“ sprach er zu ihr, „ich verschmachte sonst.“
sentences.l: “Do give me a night’s lodging and a little food and drink,” he said to her, “otherwise I am famishing.”
sentences.i: “Give me a night’s lodging and a little to eat and drink,” he said to her, “or I shall faint away.”
sentences.n: doch in an imperative is a softener with a push behind it, “do give me.” Essen und Trinken are infinitives used as nouns, “eating and drinking.” verschmachten is to languish from hunger or thirst; the present tense stands for what is about to happen.

sentences.t: „Oho!“ antwortete sie, „wer gibt einem verlaufenen Soldaten etwas? doch will ich barmherzig sein und dich aufnehmen, wenn du thust was ich verlange.“
sentences.l: “Oho!” she answered, “who gives a strayed soldier anything? yet I will be merciful and take you in, if you do what I demand.”
sentences.i: “Oho!” she answered, “who gives anything to a stray soldier? Still, I will be merciful and take you in, if you do what I ask.”
sentences.n: verlaufen as an adjective means strayed, run off from where one belongs — said of a stray dog as readily as of a discharged soldier, and not kindly meant. aufnehmen is separable, its prefix waiting at the end of the clause. thust is the 1857 spelling of tust.

sentences.t: „Was verlangst du?“ fragte der Soldat.
sentences.l: “What do you demand?” asked the soldier.
sentences.n: verlangen covers both asking for and demanding; in the witch’s mouth a moment ago it was the harder sense, and the soldier’s question keeps her word.

sentences.t: „Daß du mir morgen meinen Garten umgräbst.“
sentences.l: “That you dig over my garden for me tomorrow.”
sentences.i: “That tomorrow you dig my garden over for me.”
sentences.n: The answer is a bare daß-clause hanging from the verlangst of the question — German can leave the main clause unsaid this way. mir is a dative of interest, “for me,” which English may drop. umgraben is separable: the um- comes to rest at the end, umgräbst.

sentences.t: Der Soldat willigte ein und arbeitete den folgenden Tag aus allen Kräften, konnte aber vor Abend nicht fertig werden.
sentences.l: The soldier consented and worked the following day with all [his] strength, could however not become finished before evening.
sentences.i: The soldier agreed and worked the next day with all his might, but could not get done before evening.
sentences.n: einwilligen is separable — willigte … ein, “consented.” aus allen Kräften is literally “out of all powers”; the bracketed [his] is supplied here because English needs a possessive where German does not. fertig werden, “to become finished,” is how German says to get done.

sentences.t: „Ich sehe wohl,“ sprach die Hexe, „daß du heute nicht weiter kannst:
sentences.l: “I see well,” said the witch, “that you cannot [go] further today:
sentences.i: “I see plainly,” said the witch, “that you can do no more today;
sentences.n: wohl here is not “well” but a modal shading, “plainly enough, I daresay.” nicht weiter kannst has no verb of motion at all — kannst carries it alone — so the literal supplies [go] in brackets. The speech continues into the next unit.

sentences.t: ich will dich noch eine Nacht behalten, dafür sollst du mir morgen ein Fuder Holz spalten und klein machen.“
sentences.l: I will keep you one more night, for that you shall split me a cartload of wood tomorrow and make [it] small.”
sentences.i: I will keep you another night, and in return you shall split a cartload of wood for me tomorrow and cut it small.”
sentences.n: will is not the future but wollen, “I intend, I am willing.” A Fuder is a cartload, as much as one waggon will carry. klein machen has no object of its own — it borrows Holz from the clause before, which the literal supplies as [it].

sentences.t: Der Soldat brauchte dazu den ganzen Tag, und Abends machte ihm die Hexe den Vorschlag noch eine Nacht zu bleiben.
sentences.l: The soldier needed the whole day for it, and in the evening the witch made him the proposal to stay one more night.
sentences.i: The soldier needed the whole day for it, and in the evening the witch proposed that he stay another night.
sentences.n: dazu, “for that,” points back to the work. einen Vorschlag machen is the set phrase for putting a proposal, and the dative ihm is the person it is made to.

sentences.t: „Du sollst mir morgen nur eine geringe Arbeit thun, hinter meinem Hause ist ein alter wasserleerer Brunnen, in den ist mir mein Licht gefallen,
sentences.l: “You shall do only a small piece of work for me tomorrow, behind my house is an old water-empty well, into it my light has fallen on me,
sentences.i: “Tomorrow you shall do me only a trifling piece of work: behind my house is an old dried-up well, and my light has fallen down into it;
sentences.n: wasserleer is a transparent compound, “water-empty,” a well gone dry. mir in ist mir mein Licht gefallen is a dative of the person concerned — the loss is hers — and German says both mir and mein where English says only “my.” The 1857 text runs its clauses together with commas where we would set semicolons.

sentences.t: es brennt blau und verlischt nicht, das sollst du mir wieder herauf holen.“
sentences.l: it burns blue and does not go out, that you shall fetch back up for me.”
sentences.i: it burns blue and never goes out, and you shall fetch it back up for me.”
sentences.n: verlöschen is to go out, of a flame. das is a demonstrative object thrown to the front — “that one you shall fetch” — leaving the verb in second place. The Licht here is the burning light itself, a lamp one can carry, not brightness in general.

sentences.t: Den andern Tag führte ihn die Alte zu dem Brunnen und ließ ihn in einem Korb hinab.
sentences.l: The next day the old woman led him to the well and let him down in a basket.
sentences.n: Den andern Tag is an accusative of time with no preposition, “on the next day.” die Alte, “the old [one],” is an adjective used as a noun. hinablassen is separable, and its hinab waits at the end.

sentences.t: Er fand das blaue Licht und machte ein Zeichen daß sie ihn wieder hinauf ziehen sollte.
sentences.l: He found the blue light and made a sign that she should draw him up again.
sentences.n: The daß-clause has no comma before it in the 1857 printing; commas are set more lightly here than modern rules require. hinaufziehen is separable, and sollte pushes it to the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Sie zog ihn auch in die Höhe, als er aber dem Rand nahe war, reichte sie die Hand hinab und wollte ihm das blaue Licht abnehmen.
sentences.l: She did draw him up into the height, but when he was near the rim, she reached the hand down and wanted to take the blue light from him.
sentences.i: She did draw him up, but when he was near the top she reached her hand down and made to take the blue light from him.
sentences.n: auch here is confirming rather than adding — “she did indeed draw him up.” nahe takes the dative, dem Rand. abnehmen with a dative object, ihm … abnehmen, is “to take away from him.” German uses the plain article die Hand where English wants “her hand.”

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sagte er und merkte ihre bösen Gedanken, „das Licht gebe ich dir nicht eher, als bis ich mit beiden Füßen auf dem Erdboden stehe.“
sentences.l: “No,” he said and marked her evil thoughts, “the light I do not give you sooner than until I stand with both feet on the ground.”
sentences.i: “No,” he said, for he saw what she was about, “I shall not give you the light until I am standing with both feet on the ground.”
sentences.n: nicht eher, als bis is a doubled construction, “not sooner than until,” where English is content with a plain “not until.” merken is to notice, to take the measure of a thing. The object stands first again: das Licht gebe ich dir.

sentences.t: Da gerieth die Hexe in Wuth, ließ ihn wieder hinab in den Brunnen fallen und gieng fort.
sentences.l: Then the witch fell into a rage, let him fall down into the well again and went off.
sentences.i: At that the witch flew into a rage, let him drop back down into the well and went off.
sentences.n: in Wuth gerathen is the set phrase for flying into a rage; gerieth is the 1857 spelling of geriet, and Wuth of Wut. fallen lassen is lassen with a bare infinitive, “to let fall.”

sentences.t: Der arme Soldat fiel ohne Schaden zu nehmen auf den feuchten Boden, und das blaue Licht brannte fort, aber was konnte ihm das helfen?
sentences.l: The poor soldier fell without taking harm onto the damp ground, and the blue light burned on, but what could that help him?
sentences.i: The poor soldier fell onto the damp ground without taking harm, and the blue light went on burning; but what good was that to him?
sentences.n: ohne … zu nehmen is the ohne-zu construction, “without taking.” fortbrennen, separable, is to go on burning. was konnte ihm das helfen is a set turn — literally “what could that help him,” our “what good was that to him.”

sentences.t: er sah wohl daß er dem Tod nicht entgehen würde.
sentences.l: he saw well that he would not escape death.
sentences.i: he saw plainly that he would not escape death.
sentences.n: entgehen takes the dative, dem Tod, “escape from death.” wohl is again the modal “plainly, well enough.” The small letter on er after the question mark is the 1857 printing, which treats the question as part of the same running sentence.

sentences.t: Er saß eine Weile ganz traurig, da griff er zufällig in seine Tasche und fand seine Tabackspfeife, die noch halb gestopft war.
sentences.l: He sat a while quite sad, then he reached by chance into his pocket and found his tobacco-pipe, which was still half stuffed.
sentences.i: He sat a while quite downcast; then he happened to reach into his pocket and found his tobacco pipe, still half filled.
sentences.n: eine Weile is an accusative of duration. in die Tasche greifen is to reach into one’s pocket. Tabackspfeife is the 1857 spelling of Tabakspfeife, and a pipe is gestopft, “stuffed,” not filled.

sentences.t: „Das soll dein letztes Vergnügen sein“ dachte er, zog sie heraus, zündete sie an dem blauen Licht an und fieng an zu rauchen.
sentences.l: “That shall be your last pleasure” he thought, drew it out, lit it at the blue light and began to smoke.
sentences.n: He addresses himself as du — the tales do this often, and it is “you,” not any solemn form. anzünden and anfangen are both separable: zündete … an, fieng … an. fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Als der Dampf in der Höhle umhergezogen war, stand auf einmal ein kleines schwarzes Männchen vor ihm und fragte „Herr was befiehlst du?“
sentences.l: When the smoke had drawn about in the cave, there stood all at once a little black mannikin before him and asked “master, what do you command?”
sentences.i: When the smoke had spread about the cave, all at once a little black mannikin stood before him and asked, “Master, what is your command?”
sentences.n: umherziehen, separable, is to drift about, and it takes sein in the perfect as verbs of motion do. Männchen is the diminutive of Mann. The mannikin says Herr but addresses him as du; a servant’s address in these tales is not the formal Sie.

sentences.t: „Was habe ich dir zu befehlen?“ erwiderte der Soldat ganz verwundert.
sentences.l: “What have I to command you?” replied the soldier, quite astonished.
sentences.i: “What have I to command you?” the soldier replied, quite astonished.
sentences.n: haben … zu with an infinitive is “to have to,” here nearer “what is there for me to command.” befehlen takes a dative of the person, dir. erwiderte appears here in its modern spelling; elsewhere this edition prints erwiederte.

sentences.t: „Ich muß alles thun,“ sagte das Männchen, „was du verlangst.“
sentences.l: “I must do everything,” said the mannikin, “that you demand.”
sentences.i: “I must do everything you ask,” said the mannikin.
sentences.n: alles, was is “everything that,” with was as the relative pronoun after alles. The speech tag drops in between the two halves, which German allows freely.

sentences.t: „Gut,“ sprach der Soldat, „so hilf mir zuerst aus dem Brunnen.“
sentences.l: “Good,” said the soldier, “then first help me out of the well.”
sentences.i: “Good,” said the soldier, “then help me out of the well first.”
sentences.n: helfen takes the dative, mir. so at the head of a clause is “then, in that case,” not “so.”

sentences.t: Das Männchen nahm ihn bei der Hand und führte ihn durch einen unterirdischen Gang, vergaß aber nicht das blaue Licht mitzunehmen.
sentences.l: The mannikin took him by the hand and led him through an underground passage, forgot however not to take the blue light along.
sentences.i: The mannikin took him by the hand and led him through an underground passage, and did not forget to bring the blue light along.
sentences.n: aber sits inside the clause, not at its head as English “however” would; the literal keeps its German place. mitnehmen is separable, and in the zu-infinitive the zu is buried inside it: mitzunehmen.

sentences.t: Es zeigte ihm unterwegs die Schätze, welche die Hexe zusammengebracht und da versteckt hatte, und der Soldat nahm so viel Gold als er tragen konnte.
sentences.l: It showed him on the way the treasures which the witch had brought together and hidden there, and the soldier took as much gold as he could carry.
sentences.i: On the way it showed him the treasures the witch had gathered and hidden there, and the soldier took as much gold as he could carry.
sentences.n: Es is the pronoun for Männchen, which is neuter because every -chen diminutive is; English wants “he.” so viel … als is the older comparison, where modern German says so viel … wie.

sentences.t: Als er oben war, sprach er zu dem Männchen „nun geh hin, bind die alte Hexe und führe sie vor das Gericht.“
sentences.l: When he was above, he said to the mannikin “now go there, bind the old witch and bring her before the court.”
sentences.i: When he was up above, he said to the mannikin, “Now go and bind the old witch, and bring her before the court.”
sentences.n: hingehen is separable — geh hin, “go there.” The three imperatives are the familiar du forms with the old -e dropped, as the tales usually print them. vor das Gericht führen is to bring someone to judgment.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so kam sie auf einem wilden Kater mit furchtbarem Geschrei schnell wie der Wind vorbei geritten,
sentences.l: Not long, and she came riding past on a wild tomcat with fearful screaming, swift as the wind,
sentences.i: It was not long before she came riding past on a wild tomcat, screaming fearfully, swift as the wind;
sentences.n: Nicht lange, so … is an elliptical turn — “not long, and then” — with so holding the place of the main clause. kam … geritten is the German way of joining motion with manner, a past participle with kommen: “came riding.” A Kater is a male cat; sie is the witch, on her way to judgment.

sentences.t: und es dauerte abermals nicht lang, so war das Männchen zurück, „es ist alles ausgerichtet“ sprach es, „und die Hexe hängt schon am Galgen.“
sentences.l: and it lasted again not long, and the mannikin was back, “it is all carried out” it said, “and the witch already hangs on the gallows.”
sentences.i: and again it was not long before the mannikin was back. “It is all done,” it said, “and the witch is hanging on the gallows already.”
sentences.n: The same so pattern as a moment ago: es dauerte nicht lang, so … is “it was not long before …”. ausrichten is to carry out an errand. abermals is an old-fashioned “once again,” which the tales keep.

sentences.t: „Herr, was befiehlst du weiter?“ fragte der Kleine.
sentences.l: “Master, what do you command further?” asked the little one.
sentences.i: “Master, what else do you command?” asked the little one.
sentences.n: der Kleine is an adjective used as a noun, “the small one,” and it is masculine here although Männchen is neuter — the tale slips between the two. weiter is “further, next.”

sentences.t: „In dem Augenblick nichts,“ antwortete der Soldat, „du kannst nach Haus gehen: sei nur gleich bei der Hand wenn ich dich rufe.“
sentences.l: “At the moment nothing,” answered the soldier, “you can go home: only be at hand at once when I call you.”
sentences.i: “Nothing at this moment,” answered the soldier, “you can go home; only be at hand the instant I call you.”
sentences.n: bei der Hand sein is the same picture as English “to be at hand.” sei is the imperative of sein. nur here is “just, only,” softening the order rather than limiting it.

sentences.t: „Es ist nichts nöthig,“ sprach das Männchen, „als daß du deine Pfeife an dem blauen Licht anzündest, dann stehe ich gleich vor dir.“
sentences.l: “Nothing is needful,” said the mannikin, “but that you light your pipe at the blue light, then I stand at once before you.”
sentences.i: “Nothing is needed,” said the mannikin, “but that you light your pipe at the blue light, and I am there before you at once.”
sentences.n: nichts … als is “nothing but,” and the als and its clause come only after the speech tag. nöthig is the 1857 spelling of nötig. The present stehe stands for what will happen, as German present often does.

sentences.t: Darauf verschwand es vor seinen Augen.
sentences.l: Thereupon it vanished before his eyes.
sentences.n: Darauf, “thereupon,” stands first and pushes the subject after the verb — the ordinary German rule that the finite verb comes second.

sentences.t: Der Soldat kehrte in die Stadt zurück, aus der er gekommen war.
sentences.l: The soldier returned into the town out of which he had come.
sentences.i: The soldier went back to the town he had come from.
sentences.n: zurückkehren is separable — kehrte … zurück. aus der keeps the preposition with its relative pronoun, where English lets the preposition fall to the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Er gieng in den besten Gasthof und ließ sich schöne Kleider machen, dann befahl er dem Wirth ihm ein Zimmer so prächtig als möglich einzurichten.
sentences.l: He went into the best inn and had fine clothes made for himself, then he ordered the innkeeper to furnish him a room as splendid as possible.
sentences.i: He went to the best inn and had fine clothes made, then ordered the landlord to fit up a room for him as splendidly as could be.
sentences.n: sich etwas machen lassen — lassen with an infinitive is “to have something done,” and the reflexive sich says it is done for him. Wirth is the 1857 spelling of Wirt. so … als möglich is the older form of so … wie möglich.

sentences.t: Als es fertig war und der Soldat es bezogen hatte, rief er das schwarze Männchen und sprach „ich habe dem König treu gedient,
sentences.l: When it was ready and the soldier had moved into it, he called the black mannikin and said “I have served the king faithfully,
sentences.i: When it was ready and the soldier had moved in, he called the black mannikin and said, “I served the king faithfully,
sentences.n: beziehen, of lodgings, is to move into them. dienen takes the dative, dem König. The speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: er aber hat mich fortgeschickt und mich hungern lassen, dafür will ich jetzt Rache nehmen.“
sentences.l: he however has sent me away and let me hunger, for that I will now take revenge.”
sentences.i: but he sent me away and let me go hungry, and for that I will now take my revenge.”
sentences.n: hungern lassen is again lassen with a bare infinitive, “to let someone go hungry”; note that in this construction the perfect of lassen is lassen, not gelassen. Rache nehmen is the set phrase, to take revenge.

sentences.t: „Was soll ich thun?“ fragte der Kleine.
sentences.l: “What am I to do?” asked the little one.
sentences.n: soll is “am I to,” asking what is wanted of him, not what he ought morally to do.

sentences.t: „Spät Abends wenn die Königstochter im Bett liegt, so bring sie schlafend hierher, sie soll Mägdedienste bei mir thun.“
sentences.l: “Late in the evening when the king’s-daughter lies in bed, then bring her here sleeping, she shall do maid’s-services with me.”
sentences.i: “Late in the evening, when the king’s daughter is in bed, bring her here asleep; she shall do maid’s work for me.”
sentences.n: so picks up the whole wenn-clause and holds the main clause’s first place — German often marks the join this way, and English simply drops it. schlafend is a present participle used as a predicate, “sleeping.” Mägdedienste is built on Magd, a serving-girl.

sentences.t: Das Männchen sprach „für mich ist das ein leichtes, für dich aber ein gefährliches Ding, wenn das heraus kommt, wird es dir schlimm ergehen.“
sentences.l: The mannikin said “for me that is an easy [thing], for you however a dangerous thing, if that comes out, it will go badly for you.”
sentences.i: The mannikin said, “For me it is an easy thing, but for you a dangerous one; if it comes out, it will go badly with you.”
sentences.n: ein leichtes has no noun of its own — it borrows Ding from the phrase that follows, so the literal supplies [thing] in brackets. es ergeht dir schlimm is an impersonal set phrase, “it goes badly for you,” with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Als es zwölf geschlagen hatte, sprang die Thüre auf, und das Männchen trug die Königstochter herein.
sentences.l: When it had struck twelve, the door sprang open, and the mannikin carried the king’s-daughter in.
sentences.i: When it had struck twelve, the door sprang open and the mannikin carried the king’s daughter in.
sentences.n: es schlägt zwölf is impersonal — the clock is never named. aufspringen and hereintragen are both separable. Thüre is the 1857 spelling of Türe.

sentences.t: „Aha, bist du da?“ rief der Soldat, „frisch an die Arbeit! geh, hol den Besen und kehr die Stube.“
sentences.l: “Aha, are you there?” cried the soldier, “briskly to the work! go, fetch the broom and sweep the room.”
sentences.i: “Aha, so you are here?” cried the soldier. “Briskly to work! Go, fetch the broom and sweep the room.”
sentences.n: frisch an die Arbeit is a set exclamation with no verb in it, “to work, and lively about it.” The imperatives geh, hol, kehr are bare du forms; du is “you,” however rough the tone.

sentences.t: Als sie fertig war, hieß er sie zu seinem Sessel kommen, streckte ihr die Füße entgegen und sprach „zieh mir die Stiefel aus,“
sentences.l: When she was finished, he bade her come to his chair, stretched the feet out toward her and said “pull my boots off for me,”
sentences.i: When she had finished, he bade her come to his chair, stretched his feet out to her and said, “Pull off my boots,”
sentences.n: heißen with a bare infinitive is “to bid someone do” a thing. entgegenstrecken is separable and takes the dative of the person, ihr. zieh mir die Stiefel aus has a dative of possession — “pull the boots off me” — where English uses a possessive.

sentences.t: warf sie ihr dann ins Gesicht, und sie mußte sie aufheben, reinigen und glänzend machen.
sentences.l: threw them then into her face, and she had to pick them up, clean them and make them shining.
sentences.i: then threw them in her face, and she had to pick them up, clean them and polish them till they shone.
sentences.n: ihr ins Gesicht is once more the dative of the person with a plain article, “into her face.” glänzend machen is “to make shining”; the German spells out what English packs into “to polish.”

sentences.t: Sie that aber alles, was er ihr befahl, ohne Widerstreben, stumm und mit halbgeschlossenen Augen.
sentences.l: But she did everything that he ordered her, without resistance, mute and with half-closed eyes.
sentences.i: But she did everything he ordered her, without resisting, silent and with half-shut eyes.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat, past of thun (modern tun). Widerstreben is a noun made from the verb widerstreben, to strive against. The tale does not explain how she is held; it says only that she neither wakes nor speaks.

sentences.t: Bei dem ersten Hahnschrei trug sie das Männchen wieder in das königliche Schloß und in ihr Bett zurück.
sentences.l: At the first cockcrow the mannikin carried her back again into the royal castle and into her bed.
sentences.i: At the first cockcrow the mannikin carried her back to the royal castle and into her bed.
sentences.n: The word order can mislead: sie is the object and das Männchen the subject, though sie stands first — the case endings, not the order, decide. zurücktragen is separable and its zurück waits to the very end. The tale spells the word Hahnschrei here and Hahnenschrei a little later; both are the cock’s crow.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen, als die Königstochter aufgestanden war, gieng sie zu ihrem Vater, und erzählte ihm sie hätte einen wunderlichen Traum gehabt,
sentences.l: The next morning, when the king’s-daughter had got up, she went to her father and told him she had had a strange dream,
sentences.i: The next morning, when the king’s daughter had risen, she went to her father and told him that she had had a strange dream:
sentences.n: hätte … gehabt is the subjunctive of reported speech: German marks that these are her words, not the narrator’s, and the verb alone does the work. You will meet it constantly in the tales. wunderlich is odd, strange — not “wonderful.”

sentences.t: „ich ward durch die Straßen mit Blitzesschnelle fortgetragen und in das Zimmer eines Soldaten gebracht,
sentences.l: “I was carried off through the streets with lightning-speed and brought into the room of a soldier,
sentences.i: “I was carried off through the streets with the speed of lightning and brought into a soldier’s room,
sentences.n: ward is the old passive auxiliary, past of werden, where modern German says wurde. Blitzesschnelle is a compound with a genitive joint in the middle, “lightning’s speed.”

sentences.t: dem mußte ich als Magd dienen und aufwarten und alle gemeine Arbeit thun, die Stube kehren und die Stiefel putzen.
sentences.l: him I had to serve as a maid and wait upon and do all common work, sweep the room and clean the boots.
sentences.i: and I had to serve him as a maid and wait on him and do all the common work, sweep the room and polish the boots.
sentences.n: dem is a demonstrative in the dative, “to that one,” picking up the soldier and standing first in its clause; dienen and aufwarten both take the dative. gemein here has its older sense of ordinary or menial, not “mean.”

sentences.t: Es war nur ein Traum, und doch bin ich so müde, als wenn ich wirklich alles gethan hätte.“
sentences.l: It was only a dream, and yet I am so tired, as if I had really done everything.”
sentences.i: It was only a dream, and yet I am as tired as if I had really done it all.”
sentences.n: als wenn with the subjunctive is “as if.” gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan.

sentences.t: „Der Traum könnte wahr gewesen sein,“ sprach der König, „ich will dir einen Rath geben,
sentences.l: “The dream could have been true,” said the king, “I will give you a piece of advice,
sentences.i: “The dream may well have been true,” said the king. “I will give you a piece of advice:
sentences.n: Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat, advice; einen Rath geben is the set phrase. The speech runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: stecke deine Tasche voll Erbsen und mache ein klein Loch in die Tasche, wirst du wieder abgeholt, so fallen sie heraus und lassen die Spur auf der Straße.“
sentences.l: stuff your pocket full of peas and make a small hole in the pocket, if you are fetched away again, then they fall out and leave the trace on the street.”
sentences.i: stuff your pocket full of peas and make a little hole in it; if you are carried off again, they will fall out and leave a trail in the street.”
sentences.n: wirst du wieder abgeholt is a condition made without wenn — German can build one by simply putting the verb first — and the so that follows answers it. ein klein Loch keeps the old uninflected adjective where modern German writes ein kleines Loch. abholen is separable, here in the passive.

sentences.t: Als der König so sprach, stand das Männchen unsichtbar dabei und hörte alles mit an.
sentences.l: As the king so spoke, the mannikin stood invisible by and listened to it all.
sentences.i: While the king was speaking, the mannikin stood by invisible and heard it all.
sentences.n: dabeistehen and mitanhören are both separable, and here they pile their prefixes up at the end: stand … dabei, hörte … mit an. mitanhören is to listen in on what is meant for others.

sentences.t: Nachts, als es die schlafende Königstochter wieder durch die Straßen trug, fielen zwar einzelne Erbsen aus der Tasche,
sentences.l: At night, when it carried the sleeping king’s-daughter through the streets again, single peas did indeed fall out of the pocket,
sentences.i: At night, when it carried the sleeping king’s daughter through the streets again, single peas did fall out of the pocket,
sentences.n: Nachts is an adverbial genitive, “of a night.” zwar … aber is a paired construction, “indeed … but,” and its aber comes only in the next unit. einzelne is “single ones, scattered ones.”

sentences.t: aber sie konnten keine Spur machen, denn das listige Männchen hatte vorher in allen Straßen Erbsen verstreut.
sentences.l: but they could make no trace, for the cunning mannikin had beforehand strewn peas in all the streets.
sentences.i: but they could leave no trail, for the cunning mannikin had strewn peas beforehand in every street.
sentences.n: denn joins two main clauses and leaves its verb in second place, unlike weil, which would send it to the end. keine Spur machen is “to make no trace,” where English wants “leave.”

sentences.t: Die Königstochter aber mußte wieder bis zum Hahnenschrei Mägdedienste thun.
sentences.l: The king’s-daughter however had to do maid’s-services again until cockcrow.
sentences.i: But the king’s daughter had to do maid’s work again until cockcrow.
sentences.n: aber stands in second place, after the subject, where English puts “but” at the head; the literal keeps its German position.

sentences.t: Der König schickte am folgenden Morgen seine Leute aus, welche die Spur suchen sollten, aber es war vergeblich,
sentences.l: The king sent out his people the following morning, who were to seek the trace, but it was in vain,
sentences.i: The next morning the king sent out his men to look for the trail, but it was in vain,
sentences.n: ausschicken is separable, and its aus waits until after the object and the time phrase. welche … sollten is a relative clause of purpose, “who were to.”

sentences.t: denn in allen Straßen saßen die armen Kinder und lasen Erbsen auf und sagten „es hat heut Nacht Erbsen geregnet.“
sentences.l: for in all the streets sat the poor children and picked peas up and said “it has rained peas this night.”
sentences.i: for in every street the poor children sat picking up peas and saying, “It rained peas last night.”
sentences.n: auflesen is separable, to gather up from the ground. es hat geregnet is impersonal, with es as a placeholder subject, exactly as English says “it rained.” heut Nacht is the night just past.

sentences.t: „Wir müssen etwas anderes aussinnen,“ sprach der König, „behalt deine Schuh an, wenn du dich zu Bett legst,
sentences.l: “We must think out something else,” said the king, “keep your shoes on when you lay yourself to bed,
sentences.i: “We must think of something else,” said the king. “Keep your shoes on when you go to bed,
sentences.n: aussinnen, separable, is to devise or contrive. anbehalten is likewise separable — behalt … an, “keep on.” sich zu Bett legen is reflexive, “to lay oneself to bed.” Schuh here is the older plural without an ending.

sentences.t: und ehe du von dort zurück kehrst, verstecke einen davon; ich will ihn schon finden.“
sentences.l: and before you return from there, hide one of them; I will find it right enough.”
sentences.i: and before you come back from there, hide one of them; I shall find it, never fear.”
sentences.n: davon, “of that, of them,” points back to the shoes. schon in ich will ihn schon finden is not “already” but a reassurance — English has no single word for it, so both layers spell it out.

sentences.t: Das schwarze Männchen vernahm den Anschlag, und als der Soldat Abends verlangte er sollte die Königstochter wieder herbei tragen, rieth es ihm ab und sagte gegen diese List wüßte es kein Mittel,
sentences.l: The black mannikin heard the plan, and when the soldier demanded in the evening it should carry the king’s-daughter here again, it advised him against it and said against this trick it knew no remedy,
sentences.i: The black mannikin overheard the plan, and when the soldier demanded that evening that it should carry the king’s daughter to him again, it advised him against it and said that it knew no remedy against this trick,
sentences.n: abrathen is separable and takes the dative of the person: rieth … ihm ab, “advised him against it”; rieth is the 1857 spelling of riet. The reported clauses stand in the subjunctive again — sollte, wüßte — which is how German keeps another’s words another’s.

sentences.t: und wenn der Schuh bei ihm gefunden würde, so könnte es ihm schlimm ergehen.
sentences.l: and if the shoe were found with him, then it could go badly for him.
sentences.i: and that if the shoe were found in his keeping, it might go badly with him.
sentences.n: bei ihm is “about him, in his keeping.” The same impersonal es ergeht ihm schlimm as before, now in the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: „Thue was ich dir sage“ erwiderte der Soldat, und die Königstochter mußte auch in der dritten Nacht wie eine Magd arbeiten;
sentences.l: “Do what I tell you” replied the soldier, and the king’s-daughter had to work like a maid in the third night too;
sentences.i: “Do what I tell you,” replied the soldier, and on the third night too the king’s daughter had to work like a serving-maid;
sentences.n: Thue is the imperative of thun, the 1857 spelling of tun, with the old full -e ending. auch belongs to in der dritten Nacht, “on the third night as well.”

sentences.t: sie versteckte aber, ehe sie zurückgetragen wurde, einen Schuh unter das Bett.
sentences.l: but she hid, before she was carried back, one shoe under the bed.
sentences.i: but before she was carried back she hid one shoe under the bed.
sentences.n: The object einen Schuh comes only after the whole ehe-clause, which German can insert between the verb and its object; English will not carry the interruption that far, so the idiomatic moves the clause to the front.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen ließ der König in der ganzen Stadt den Schuh seiner Tochter suchen:
sentences.l: The next morning the king had his daughter’s shoe sought in the whole town:
sentences.i: The next morning the king had search made for his daughter’s shoe through the whole town:
sentences.n: lassen with an infinitive again, “had [someone] search.” The searchers are never named, which is why English reaches for a passive.

sentences.t: er ward bei dem Soldaten gefunden, und der Soldat selbst, der sich auf Bitten des Kleinen zum Thor hinaus gemacht hatte, ward bald eingeholt und ins Gefängnis geworfen.
sentences.l: it was found with the soldier, and the soldier himself, who at the little one’s entreaty had made himself out through the gate, was soon overtaken and thrown into prison.
sentences.i: it was found in the soldier’s keeping, and the soldier himself, who at the little one’s urging had made off out of the gate, was soon overtaken and thrown into prison.
sentences.n: er is “it,” the shoe — der Schuh is masculine, so its pronoun is er. sich hinausmachen is “to make off, take oneself out.” auf Bitten is “at the entreaty of.” Thor is the 1857 spelling of Tor, a gate.

sentences.t: Er hatte sein Bestes bei der Flucht vergessen, das blaue Licht und das Gold, und hatte nur noch einen Dukaten in der Tasche.
sentences.l: He had forgotten his best in the flight, the blue light and the gold, and had only one ducat left in his pocket.
sentences.i: In his flight he had forgotten the best he had, the blue light and the gold, and had only one ducat left in his pocket.
sentences.n: sein Bestes is an adjective used as a noun, “his best [thing].” nur noch is “only … left.” A ducat is a gold coin, so a single one is not nothing — but nothing beside what he left behind.

sentences.t: Als er nun mit Ketten belastet an dem Fenster seines Gefängnisses stand, sah er einen seiner Kameraden vorbeigehen.
sentences.l: When he now stood laden with chains at the window of his prison, he saw one of his comrades go past.
sentences.i: As he stood there laden with chains at the window of his prison, he saw one of his comrades go past.
sentences.n: belastet is a past participle used adjectivally, “laden.” sehen with a bare infinitive, sah … vorbeigehen, is “saw him go past.” nun in a narrative als-clause is little more than “now, at this point.”

sentences.t: Er klopfte an die Scheibe, und als er herbeikam, sagte er „sei so gut und hol mir das kleine Bündelchen, das ich in dem Gasthaus habe liegen lassen, ich gebe dir dafür einen Dukaten.“
sentences.l: He knocked on the pane, and when he came up, he said “be so good and fetch me the little bundle that I have let lie in the inn, I give you a ducat for it.”
sentences.i: He knocked on the pane, and when the man came up he said, “Be so good as to fetch me the little bundle I left lying at the inn; I will give you a ducat for it.”
sentences.n: The er of the second clause could be either man; the sense makes the comrade the one who comes up, and the idiomatic says so. liegen lassen keeps its infinitive form in the perfect instead of taking ge-, the same rule as hungern lassen earlier. Bündelchen is a diminutive of Bündel, itself already a small thing.

sentences.t: Der Kamerad lief hin, und brachte ihm das Verlangte.
sentences.l: The comrade ran there and brought him the demanded [thing].
sentences.i: The comrade ran off and brought him what he had asked for.
sentences.n: das Verlangte is a past participle used as a noun, “the thing demanded”; the literal supplies [thing] in brackets because English cannot leave it bare. hinlaufen is separable.

sentences.t: Sobald der Soldat wieder allein war, steckte er seine Pfeife an und ließ das schwarze Männchen kommen.
sentences.l: As soon as the soldier was alone again, he lit his pipe and had the black mannikin come.
sentences.i: As soon as the soldier was alone again he lit his pipe and made the black mannikin come.
sentences.n: anstecken, separable, is to light. lassen with an infinitive is here nearer “made” than “let” — German uses the one verb for both.

sentences.t: „Sei ohne Furcht,“ sprach es zu seinem Herrn, „geh hin wo sie dich hinführen und laß alles geschehen, nimm nur das blaue Licht mit.“
sentences.l: “Be without fear,” it said to its master, “go there where they lead you and let everything happen, only take the blue light along.”
sentences.i: “Have no fear,” it said to its master. “Go where they lead you and let everything happen; only take the blue light with you.”
sentences.n: hingehen and hinführen both carry hin, “thither,” the direction away from the speaker, which English does not mark. mitnehmen is separable: nimm … mit.

sentences.t: Am anderen Tag ward Gericht über den Soldaten gehalten, und obgleich er nichts Böses gethan hatte, verurtheilte ihn der Richter doch zum Tode.
sentences.l: The next day court was held over the soldier, and although he had done nothing evil, the judge yet condemned him to death.
sentences.i: The next day judgment was held over the soldier, and although he had done nothing wrong, the judge condemned him to death all the same.
sentences.n: Gericht halten über is the set phrase for holding a trial over someone. nichts Böses is an adjective used as a noun after nichts, “nothing evil.” doch answering obgleich is “yet, all the same.” verurtheilte is the 1857 spelling of verurteilte.

sentences.t: Als er nun hinaus geführt wurde, bat er den König um eine letzte Gnade.
sentences.l: When he was now led out, he asked the king for a last favour.
sentences.i: As he was being led out, he begged a last favour of the king.
sentences.n: bitten um is “to ask for,” with the person in the accusative — den König — and the thing after um. Gnade is a grace or favour granted from above, the same word as mercy.

sentences.t: „Was für eine?“ fragte der König.
sentences.l: “What kind of one?” asked the king.
sentences.i: “What favour?” asked the king.
sentences.n: was für ein is the set question “what kind of”; the für in it is not the preposition “for,” and eine stands alone in place of the noun Gnade.

sentences.t: „Daß ich auf dem Weg noch eine Pfeife rauchen darf.“
sentences.l: “That I may smoke one more pipe on the way.”
sentences.n: Another bare daß-clause hanging from the unspoken question, as in the witch’s answer near the beginning. noch eine is “one more.” dürfen is permission, “may,” not ability.

sentences.t: „Du kannst drei rauchen,“ antwortete der König, „aber glaube nicht daß ich dir das Leben schenke.“
sentences.l: “You can smoke three,” answered the king, “but do not believe that I grant you your life.”
sentences.i: “You may smoke three,” answered the king, “but do not imagine that I am sparing your life.”
sentences.n: jemandem das Leben schenken is the set phrase for sparing a life — literally “to make someone a present of his life,” with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Da zog der Soldat seine Pfeife heraus und zündete sie an dem blauen Licht an,
sentences.l: Then the soldier drew his pipe out and lit it at the blue light,
sentences.i: Then the soldier drew out his pipe and lit it at the blue light,
sentences.n: Two separable verbs in a row, herausziehen and anzünden, each leaving its prefix at the end of its clause.

sentences.t: und wie ein paar Ringel von Rauch aufgestiegen waren, so stand schon das Männchen da, hatte einen kleinen Knüppel in der Hand und sprach „was befiehlt mein Herr?“
sentences.l: and when a couple of rings of smoke had risen up, there already stood the mannikin, had a small cudgel in the hand and said “what does my master command?”
sentences.i: and when a few rings of smoke had gone up, there stood the mannikin already, a small cudgel in his hand, and said, “What does my master command?”
sentences.n: Ringel is a little ring or curl. The mannikin now says mein Herr in the third person, a shade more ceremonious than the du of its first appearance. dastehen is separable: stand … da.

sentences.t: „Schlag mir da die falschen Richter und ihre Häscher zu Boden, und verschone auch den König nicht, der mich so schlecht behandelt hat.“
sentences.l: “Strike there for me the false judges and their catchpoles to the ground, and do not spare the king either, who has treated me so badly.”
sentences.i: “Strike those false judges and their bailiffs to the ground for me, and do not spare the king either, who has treated me so badly.”
sentences.n: mir is an ethical dative — not an object at all, but a “for me, if you please” thrown into the order. Häscher are the officers who seize and hold a prisoner, a harsher word than bailiff. zu Boden schlagen is the set phrase for felling someone.

sentences.t: Da fuhr das Männchen wie der Blitz, zickzack, hin und her, und wen es mit seinem Knüppel nur anrührte, der fiel schon zu Boden, und getraute sich nicht mehr zu regen.
sentences.l: Then the mannikin darted like the lightning, zigzag, to and fro, and whomever it only touched with its cudgel, he fell down at once and did not dare stir himself any more.
sentences.i: Then the mannikin darted like lightning, zigzag, to and fro, and whomever it so much as touched with its cudgel fell to the ground at once and dared not stir again.
sentences.n: wen … der is the old correlative, “whomever … he.” nur here means “so much as, merely,” not “only.” sich getrauen and sich regen are both reflexive; anrühren is separable.

sentences.t: Dem König ward angst, er legte sich auf das Bitten und um nur das Leben zu behalten gab er dem Soldat das Reich und seine Tochter zur Frau.
sentences.l: To the king came fear, he laid himself to entreaty and, only to keep his life, gave the soldier the kingdom and his daughter to wife.
sentences.i: The king took fright; he fell to entreating, and only to keep his life he gave the soldier the kingdom and his daughter to wife.
sentences.n: mir wird angst is impersonal with the person in the dative — fear comes upon the king rather than the king being afraid. sich auf das Bitten legen is to set about pleading in earnest. zur Frau geben is the formula for giving a woman in marriage. dem Soldat drops the weak ending the noun usually takes, dem Soldaten.

glossary.bind: binden — to bind (imperative sg., with the old -e dropped: bind for binde)
glossary.blitz: der Blitz — lightning (wie der Blitz, like lightning)
glossary.diese: dieser — this (fem. acc. sg. here: diese List)
glossary.ketten: die Kette — chain (dat. pl. here: mit Ketten belastet)
glossary.kleine: klein — little, small (inflected; der Kleine, the little one, the adjective used as a noun)
glossary.kommt: kommen — to come (3rd sg. present; here herauskommen, to come out, come to light)
glossary.licht: das Licht — light; also a light one can carry or set down, a lamp or flame
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldier (a weak noun: Soldaten is dat./acc. sg. as well as the plural)
